Hi! On behalf of the Mathlib Initiative I want to share some automation we've been building on top of the hopscotch tool (presented a few weeks ago on this Zulip thread).

The goal here is twofold:
(1) provide the ecosystem with flexible mechanisms to stay up to date with the latest development in the library,
(2) have a birds-eye-view of the 'ecosystem health' with respect to compatibility

Background

hopscotch is an interactive CLI that can be used to pinpoint a breaking change in a dependency: it will binary search through the dependency's version history and find the first change incompatible with the project (the 'culprit' of an 'incompatibility'). Read more about it in the repo README.

The intended workflow for local usage of this tool is to fix 'incompatible' revisions in your downstream one by one until getting to a 'target' revision (hopefully, the tip of mathlib's master branch).

On the other hand, the tool can be used in a continuous integration fashion to both stay up to date with the latest changes in the library (thus avoiding incompatible changes of your own) and also react quickly to new incompatibilities.

We have built some automation precisely for GitHub-hosted Lean projects for these purposes, with automated bumping and alerting through pull requests and GitHub issues.

hopscotch-action

hopscotch-action is a reusable GitHub Action that wraps the hopscotch CLI to:

  • Run it and identify the culprit of an incompatibility. Bisect an upstream dependency's commit history to find a commit that introduced the incompatibility.
  • Open a bump PR: When the build passes (or after finding the last-good commit), automatically open or update a pull request to advance the manifest pin.
  • Track incompatibilities with an issue: after finding a culprit, automatically open or update an issue to report the breaking commit.

Use it in a GitHub workflow like so:

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: leanprover-community/hopscotch-action@v1
        with:
          dependency: mathlib
          to: master
          open-pr: true     # defaults to true
          open-issue: true  # defaults to true
          pr-labels: "dependencies,auto-bump"

(Note this is agnostic to mathlib, and it could be used with another dependency in the lakefile)

Here's an example auto-bump PR opened by the action:

and an example issue informing the 'first known bad' revision:

2. downstream-reports

A related project is downstream-reports: a reporting platform built on top of hopscotch that runs automatic break detection for a selected set of mathlib downstream projects. Mathlib intends to use this service to monitor ecosystem health: you can see the current "compatibility state" of these projects against the latest mathlib changes in https://leanprover-community.github.io/downstream-reports/. This repository also provides some companion actions to consume this data from the downstream projects in question.

The functionality provided by downstream-reports is basically the same as hopscotch-action, but hosted on leanprover-community infrastructure, providing centralized monitoring and producing historical data.

Also, special thanks to downstream maintainers that provided valuable early feedback while developing these tools: Yaël Dillies, Chris Henson, Joseph Tooby-Smith, Michael Rothgang, Pietro Monticone :)
As I said in the CSLib channel, thank you so much for your work on this! I love seeing the Mathlib Initiative put thoughtful work into soliciting feedback and developing tooling for downstream users.

Just seconding what Chris said -- this is working super-well for FLT. My old workflow was "wait about a week, then bump, then notice that several independent things are broken, then try to figure out why". Now it's "get notified the instant something is broken together with a link to the precise PR which broke it, making fixing it much much easier".
@Marcelo Lynch are you looking for more projects to add to https://leanprover-community.github.io/downstream-reports/ or the current ones are enough to show how it works?
@Riccardo Brasca It's open to onboarding any downstreams that would benefit from it -- do send me a DM and I can assist you in customizing it for your needs

The Hopscotch-powered downstream-reports actions are working great on my repo. I have one feature request though: @Marcelo Lynch would it be possible to have PRs that bump to a Mathlib tag if there is a new one? I'd like to make sure that my v4.32.0 tag is exactly at the same Mathlib commit as Mathlib's v4.32.0 tag. To ensure maximal compatibility if other projects import it.

So if my project depends on commit 69aaaa3 and the current latest Mathlib is at b438433, but there is a new Mathlib tag v4.32.0 between those (such that the order is 69aaaa3 -> ... -> v4.32.0 -> ... b438433), I'd like the action to open two PRs: one to bump to the tag, and another one to bump to the latest commit. Then I'm free to merge the one I want.

@Rémy Degenne This is possible by querying 'last-good-release', which is something that downstream-reports publishes too: see LML#150.

I could also make this a 'first class' feature, namely add some parameter that makes 'bump to latest' adopt this behavior. I hesitate in adding more and more parameters for specific scenarios (especially if they can be handled in other ways like here), but it seems like this might be a reasonable 'wish' for a maintainer in general.

Somewhat relatedly, is it possible to configure not bumping across toolchains? In CSLib for example, we have been asked by the FRO to allow them to open the toolchain bump PRs, so right now I manually make sure the hopscotch PRs don't go across a release.
Pragmatically you could achieve it this same way because the tags correspond to toolchain bumps
Or, say, skipping the 'open PR' step if there is a diff in lean-toolchain

Thanks a lot for the PR!

I think this behaviour of stopping at tags should really be the default. Right now in the Lean project ecosystem importing two projects A and B that both depend on Mathlib (or other significant dependencies) into a project C is a recipe for disaster.
The tag system is supposed to alleviate that problem, but it only works well if tags in A and B point to the same Mathlib commit. I think that automated tooling provided by the community like the downstream-reports actions should try and ensure that compatibility by default.

I think we should probably support this per-repository in the downstreams-report inventory configuration. The system always chooses a "target" commit of mathlib to advance to. Today, this is always the tip of mathlib master. We could add a setting that says "<for this downstream> make the bump target the next tagged release after the pinned version in its lake-manifest".

This way, there is no need to do any of this arithmetic with 'last good release' -- the published 'last known good' for that repo is always bounded by the next tag. The only downside is that you won't detect issues beyond that tag until you merge the bump.

An option in the downstream-reports configuration would be nice!
It would be even better if it was on by default :) That way people adding projects would not have to know about it to have a tag compatible with other projects in the ecosystem.
yep, sounds good to me
But note that this won't automatically tag the bump, that depends on the project
Oh yes, I'm assuming that they also use the lean-release-tag action.
Which makes me think that we could have a page that lists all the nice github actions that one would want to use in their repository, if we don't have one already that I don't know about.
I didn't even know about that one :-)

Marcelo Lynch said:

I think we should probably support this per-repository in the downstreams-report inventory configuration. The system always chooses a "target" commit of mathlib to advance to. Today, this is always the tip of mathlib master. We could add a setting that says "<for this downstream> make the bump target the next tagged release after the pinned version in its lake-manifest".

This way, there is no need to do any of this arithmetic with 'last good release' -- the published 'last known good' for that repo is always bounded by the next tag. The only downside is that you won't detect issues beyond that tag until you merge the bump.

I've merged this change to downstream-reports and made it the default -- this way, tagged releases will always we marked/published as a "last-known-good" at some point unless the project 'manually' bumps beyond them.
What if I disabled lkg bumps? Do I still get PRs to tagged releases?
Surely it would make most sense if lkg, fkb and tagged releases were the three kinds of commits you could bump to, and they could be enabled independently of each other

I still think the rationale should be to bump as often as possible. Stopping at a release for the whole "cross package compatibility" story makes sense to me but it doesn't take that away. If you want to not merge the PRs until they correspond to a tag (the PR will be autoupdated until that happens, and then it won't anymore, because the target remains "the next release"), then you can make that choice
But bump-to-latest does admit a "last good release" query-type which will only bump to release tags
